title: Replacing people and things
goal: Use object pronouns like a real Brazilian — including the form language teachers cross out but a hundred million people say every day.

notes: ⚠️ **Eu não conheço ele is wrong according to the grammar books, and right according to Brazil.** The standard rule demands *não o conheço*. But to Brazilian ears that sounds like a 1970s newsreader. What everyone says every day, across all walks of life, is *eu conheço ele*, *eu vi ele*, *eu encontrei ela*. This module teaches the second — because that's what you'll hear and what will get you understood.

**Te is used for "you", even though the pronoun is você.** Grammatically this is a mix: *você* should pair with *lhe*, and *te* belongs to *tu*. But Brazilians use *te* with *você* without a second thought: *eu te ligo*, *ele te viu*, *te amo*. This isn't a mistake to avoid — it's Brazilian Portuguese.

**Me desculpa, not desculpe-me.** Notice once again that the little pronoun goes **before** the verb in Brazil. This holds almost without exception in conversation, even at the start of a sentence — something the standard rules actually forbid.
**Pra você, pra mim.** The spoken form of *para*. Notice that the pronoun after a preposition is different from the one before a verb: not *pra me* but **pra mim**.

**Que fofa!** = "so sweet!" — typical Brazilian praise for a kind gesture. *Fofo/fofa* literally means "fluffy", and it's used for anything adorable. And **Fechado!** literally "closed", means "deal, agreed" — in the same family as *combinado*.

grammars.title: Pronouns before the verb
body: Three forms you need to master, and in Brazilian Portuguese they all go **before** the verb.
after: **For the third person, Brazil uses the ordinary pronoun after the verb**: *Eu vi **ele***, *Eu conheço **ela***, *Eu encontrei **eles***. The standard forms *o*, *a*, *os*, *as* still appear in formal writing and books, so learn to recognize them — but don't force yourself to use them.
⚠️ One standard form that stays alive: **lhe** for "to him/her/you" in formal letters and polite address. As a beginner you don't need it at all.

grammars.title: Pronouns after prepositions
body: Yet another set of forms, and only the first two rows really break the pattern.
after: **Comigo and conosco are two fused words that survived from Latin.** There's no *com mim* — that form is wrong. Learn both as whole words.

⚠️ **Para mim, not para eu.** This is the most common beginner mistake, and also the easiest to avoid once you notice it. Rule of thumb: after any preposition, "I" becomes *mim* — just as English says "for me", not "for I".

grammars.title: Verbs that demand a preposition
body: Some Portuguese verbs always pair with a particular preposition, and the partner often doesn't match English.
after: You've already met the first three rows in earlier units. What matters is the general pattern: **the preposition sticks to the verb**, not to the meaning. Learn *gostar de* as one word, not as *gostar* + a rule.
*Sonhar com você* = "to dream about you" — it's also the title of several Brazilian songs, so you'll hear it.

blocks.text: **Me liga!** is the most typically Brazilian way to say goodbye. It's a command, but the tone is warm — roughly "keep in touch". Its partner: *Qualquer coisa, me chama* ("if you need anything, give me a shout").
Notice *Me passa o sal?* — a question that is really a softened command. Adding *por favor* makes it perfect, but Brazilians often get by with just a rising tone of voice.

sections.title: Standard and spoken side by side

blocks.text: This table isn't for memorizing but for recognizing. You'll meet the left column in books and letters; you'll hear the right column in the street.

⚠️ Don't conclude that the right column is "wrong". A language spoken by a hundred and twenty million educated adults every day isn't a mistake — it's a different register. All you need to know is when to use which: the right column for talking, the left column for writing a job application.

items: Do you know where the bank is? → *Você sabe onde fica o banco?*
I have to go now → *Eu tenho que ir agora*
I need money → *Eu preciso de dinheiro*
Can you pay by card? → *Dá para pagar no cartão?*
